steps.title: State the decision rule
steps.detail: Accept the lot if the sample contains 3 defects or fewer; reject it above 3.

steps.title: Inspect the sample
steps.detail: 125 units are inspected and 2 defects are found.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.detail: 2 is within the acceptance number of 3, so the lot passes.

data.title: Accepting a lot of 1,000 units
data.caption: Acceptance sampling balances inspection cost against the risk of accepting defective products.
data.scenario: Acceptance sampling decides a whole lot from a sample of it, so the plan has to say how big the sample is and how many defects it will tolerate before the lot is rejected.
data.takeaway: Two risks remain whatever the plan: the producer's risk \(\alpha\) of rejecting a good lot, and the consumer's risk \(\beta\) of accepting a bad one. Typical targets are \(\alpha = 0.05\) and \(\beta = 0.10\).

steps.title: Trace every path through the network
steps.detail: Each activity has exactly one predecessor, so there is one path: A to B to C to D to E.

steps.title: Take the longest path as critical
steps.detail: It is the only path, so every activity on it is critical and none has slack.

data.title: Finding the critical path of a five-activity project
data.result: 12 weeks, along the critical path A → B → C → D → E.
data.caption: CPM identifies the sequence of activities that determines how long a project takes.
data.scenario: Each activity depends on the one before it, so the project cannot finish sooner than the longest chain of them takes.
data.takeaway: A delay to any activity on the critical path delays the whole project. Activities off it have slack and can slip by that much without doing so.

steps.title: Generate the arrivals
steps.detail: Draw arrival times from an exponential distribution.

steps.title: Serve or queue each arrival
steps.detail: If the server is idle, service starts at once; if it is busy, the customer joins the queue.

steps.title: Release the server on completion
steps.detail: Start the next customer if the queue is not empty, otherwise the server goes idle.

steps.title: Track the measures that matter
steps.detail: Wait time, service time, queue length and server utilisation.

data.title: Simulating a single-server service counter
data.result:
Average wait 2.3 minutes.
Average queue length 0.8 customers.
Server utilisation 83%.
data.caption: Discrete event simulation models queuing systems to evaluate service capacity.
data.scenario: Arrivals and service times vary, so the queue cannot be worked out with one calculation. A simulation runs the system event by event and measures what actually happens.
data.takeaway: A second server would cut the average wait to about 0.1 minutes — the queue is driven by how close utilisation is to capacity, not by the average arrival rate alone.
